The Fall of Constantinople. On the twenty-ninth of May, fourteen fifty-three, Constantinople—the capital of the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years—fell to Ottoman forces under Mehmed II. The siege lasted fifty-three days, from early April to the end of May. A Byzantine garrison of perhaps five to seven thousand defended desperately against an Ottoman force of fifty to eighty thousand.

Mehmed the Conqueror, as he came to be known, brought innovative cannon and artillery to bear against the Theodosian Walls, those famed fortifications that had protected the city for centuries. Wave after wave the artillery battered the ancient stones. The final breach came, and in the last moments, the Byzantine Emperor Constantine XI Palaiogus died fighting on the walls. His body was never found, lost in the chaos of the final assault. With him died the last emperor of a dynasty that had endured since the days of Rome itself.

The conquest was achieved through more than firepower. Mehmed offered generous terms to those who surrendered, psychological pressure that encouraged capitulation. The fall triggered a mass emigration of Byzantine scholars to Western Europe, carrying precious manuscripts and classical knowledge that fuelled the European Renaissance. The city became Istanbul, capital of the Ottoman Empire, and remained under Ottoman rule for nearly five hundred years. The conquest fundamentally reshaped the religious and political map of the Mediterranean. The medieval world had ended, and the modern era had begun on the walls of an ancient city.
